title: Life and dignity
hookLine: a psalm looks at the stars, then at people, and finds a crown

lines: THE MOON, THE STARS, AND A PERSON.
cards: A psalm stands under the night sky, looks at the moon and the stars, and asks a question. In the Douay-Rheims: "What is man that thou art mindful of him?" Next to all that sky, a person looks small.

Then the psalm answers its own question, and the answer goes the other way: "Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, thou hast crowned him with glory and honour." Not small after all. Crowned.
Catholic social teaching sets that crown on every head before it says a word about wages or laws. Today, life and dignity.

teach.b: First, the root. Genesis says, in the Douay-Rheims: "God created man to his own image." Catholics read that line as the ground under this whole block.
Dignity isn't a prize a society hands out. It comes with being human.
Second, it isn't earned, and it can't be lost: not by being unproductive, or sick, or old, or poor, or in prison, or not yet born.
The Catechism, quoting the Second Vatican Council, says God willed each human being for their own sake, not as a tool for something else. Third, the span.

The Church teaches that every human life is to be protected from conception to natural death. That's why Catholic teaching opposes abortion and euthanasia, and why the Catechism now calls the death penalty inadmissible.
The same council also named slavery, the selling of women and children, and disgraceful working conditions as attacks on human dignity.
Some Catholics give their energy to one end of that span and some to another; the teaching holds the whole line together. Fourth, the test.

teach.h: ONE OF THESE MY LEAST BRETHREN.
teach.b: In Matthew, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."
Dignity gets tested at the edges, with the people easiest to overlook: the newborn and the dying, the man asleep in a doorway, the coworker nobody says good morning to.

how: Catholics act on this teaching through pro-life ministries, hospice and hospital care, prison visiting, work against human trafficking, and campaigns against the death penalty; some parishes keep days of prayer for the dignity of life.

o: the right to live however you choose, without limits
the respect a person earns through hard, honest work
every person's worth, from conception to natural death

games.q: life and dignity — tap the pairs.
p: a little less than the angels
the psalm under the night sky
one of these my least brethren

s: in Catholic teaching, a person's dignity depends on what they contribute
dignity comes with being human, made in God's image; it isn't earned and can't be lost.
the Second Vatican Council named disgraceful working conditions as an attack on human dignity
the Catechism now calls the death penalty inadmissible
it counts it among the things that contradict the dignity of the person.

games.q: you're the psalm singer under the night sky, moon and stars overhead. you ask what a human being is. what's the psalm's answer?
o: a little less than the angels, crowned with glory.
games.why: a little less than the angels, crowned with glory. the question starts small and the answer ends with a crown.

practice: Bring to mind someone you'll cross today who's easy to overlook, the cashier, the person who cleans the office after everyone leaves, an elderly neighbor, someone you're annoyed with, and hold their face for a moment.
Choose one concrete way to honor them: their name used, eye contact held, a real question asked and the answer actually heard. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Life and dignity. The Church's first principle here: every person is made in God's image, and every life is to be protected from conception to natural death. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: image of God. the Church's phrase for what Genesis says every person is made in.

carryVoice: Your line: every life. A crown on every head, earned by no one and lost by no one. Go gently.
